patch.value: The graph node floor counts materialized placeholders, so its negative control declares the fully repaired corpus a failure and the gate passes only while a dangling reference exists

The graph node floor is denominated over a population that excludes assembly-materialized placeholder nodes, so repairing a dangling reference can never lower it; The negative control for every structural floor is stated over a population the project would accept as correct, so no passing condition requires a known defect to be present; A repair that removes a meaningless edge or node is distinguishable at the gate from an erosion that removes recorded work, without a hand edit to the declaration; The graph audit's four legacy remediation codes can be executed to zero with every block-enforcement assurance gate still passing, proven by running them; Placeholder-inclusive node counts remain available as a diagnostic measurement and are explicitly marked as unsuitable as a ratchet basis
A structural floor is denominated over the population the project intends to preserve, so executing a prescribed repair can never fail it
Governance is only worth running if its verdict tracks the thing it claims to protect. A floor that requires broken data inverts that: the safest tracker state is the one the gate rejects.
Blocks the entire legacy graph hygiene programme: three of pm-hnc9w7's four acceptance criteria cannot be satisfied without failing a block-enforcement gate.
Node and edge floors are denominated over real recorded items and real stored edges; placeholder-inclusive counts remain a diagnostic and are never a ratchet basis.
Demonstrated live this session, not argued: executing the audit's own prescribed remediation drove a block-enforcement gate from pass to fail.

author: harness:claude-code

patch.value:
## Measured this session, in order

Starting state: `pm graph audit` reported 11 findings across four legacy codes; `pm assurance run tracker-context-quality --trigger ci` reported `verdict: pass`. Graph profile: 2,458 nodes, of which 3 were assembly-materialized placeholders for dangling references (`missing_nodes: 3`), and 12,116 edges.

Executed exactly the remediation the audit prescribes, on three of its four codes:

- 8 duplicated `child` spellings collapsed onto the canonical `parent` edge each child already stored (`legacy_duplicate_edge` 8 to 0);
- 3 dangling references removed: one dependency row to an item that does not exist, and two legacy free-text `blocked_by` scalars that were never item ids (`missing_reference_terminal` 3 to 0);
- 98 retired `no-active-blocker` sentinel scalars cleared (`legacy_no_blocker_sentinel` 98 to 0).

Resulting state: 8 findings, all of one remaining code. Graph profile: 2,455 nodes, `missing_nodes: 0`, 12,105 edges. `pm assurance run tracker-context-quality --trigger ci` now reports `verdict: block`, `exit_code: 1`, on `graph-nodes-floor`: observed 2455, floor 2456, distance -1, enforcement `block`.

The three nodes that disappeared are exactly the three placeholders. The corpus of real recorded items did not change.

## The declaration says so in its own words

`pm assurance show measurement graph-nodes` describes its source as "All indexed graph nodes including missing placeholders" and reads `profile.nodes` from the audit.

`pm assurance show assertion graph-nodes-floor` carries `floor: 2456` and this negative control:

```
negative_control:
  cases[2]{observed,expected}:
    2456,pass
    2455,fail
```

There are 2,455 real items. The negative control therefore states that a corpus containing every recorded item and zero dangling references must fail. The floor is satisfiable only while at least one reference points at an item that does not exist.

## Why this is a second instance, not a restatement

pm-9gzr4r owns the edge-count floor being denominated over a population that includes the edges the graph itself calls redundant. That is an argument about redundancy. This is a different measurement (`graph-nodes`), a different assertion owner (pm-o2kc), and a different mechanism: placeholder materialization during assembly, which is a deliberate feature so bounded traversals can explain absent work rather than silently dropping it. The feature is correct. Ratcheting a floor over its output is what is wrong.

## The edge floor blocks the fourth code as well

`graph-edges-floor` is 12103 with `enforcement: block`; observed is 12105, so headroom is 2 edges. The remaining legacy code is 8 terminal ordering cycles across 49 items, whose root cause is 26 holders that each store a legacy scalar `blocked_by: X` together with a contradicting structured row `X, blocks`. Removing those 26 inverted rows takes edges to 12,079 and fails the floor by 24.

So all four of pm-hnc9w7's remediation criteria are individually blocked by a total-count floor. The finding-count ceilings in the same registry behave correctly and reward the same cleanup: `graph-finding-legacy-duplicate-edge` (ceiling 8), `legacy-no-blocker-sentinel` (98), `missing-reference-terminal` (3) all moved to 0 and still pass. Two families of declarations in one registry disagree about whether cleanup is progress.

## Boundary

The fix is the denominator, not the numbers. Raising or lowering a floor by hand is the erosion this class is supposed to detect, so the repair must make removal-of-meaningless and removal-of-meaningful structurally distinguishable at the gate.
